newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian winemakers still hope for good vintage.
newsitem.headline: Australian winemakers still hope for good vintage.

text.p: Australian winemakers say looming drought conditions may cut back expected tonnages for the 1998 vintage, but they believe lessons learnt from the disastrous 1994-95 drought should mitigate losses.
Australia's biggest winemaker, Southcorp Wines, a division of Southcorp Holdings Ltd, said on Monday that drought conditions could affect up to 20 percent of its vineyards.
However the division's chief executive, Bruce Kemp, said it was far too early for any predictions on tonnages with the vintage not properly underway until March 1998.

Other major producers Orlando Wyndham and BRL Hardy Ltd said they still expected 1998 production to well exceed this year's crush of 800,000 tonnes of grapes and, if conditions improved, to beat the record 880,000 tonnes crushed in 1996.
Buoyed by ever-growing exports, the industry earlier this year said it anticipated a 1998 crush of around 900,000 tonnes.

Low rainfall through much of agricultural Australia since April has sparked fears of an El Nino-related drought and, for winemakers, brought back memories of the distrastrous 1995 vintage when only 630,000 tonnes of grapes were crushed.

While the vast majority of Australian vineyards have access to irrigation, winemakers are concerned about dryland areas, such as the parts of the premium Barossa Valley, McLaren Vale and Clare Valley regions which rely on surface water collection.

"If we do not have rain by the end of August, I would start to get concerned, not for the industry overall but for certain parts of it," said Philip Laffer, chief winemaker with Orlando, part of the French-based Pernod Ricard.
However, he told Reuters one lesson from 1994-95 had been for grapegrowers in irrigation areas to begin watering in winter to ensure adequate soil moisture for bud-burst in spring.

This remedial action - coupled with the biennial cropping pattern of grapes which was expected to lift yields in 1998, plus increased tonnages from further new plantings coming on stream - would minimise the impact Australia-wide, he said.
"There would be some districts perhaps that are harder hit than others, but (overall) I think it would be very unlikely to have a vintage smaller than 1997," Laffer said.
"If we get rain in August, September, we will have a record vintage, absolutely," he said.

BRL operations and technical director Angus Kennedy said he expected the 1998 vintage to be substantially more than in 1997, regardless of drought conditions, with his company expecting its crush to rise to 165,000 tonnes, up from 1997's 135,000.
Kennedy said he believed around 10 percent of BRL's vineyards relied on surface water collection and these could be hit by a 30 percent drop in anticipated tonnages if rainfall remained low.
"Certainly a drought, losing 5-10 percent of the potential crop, is not inconceivable but it is also manageable," he said.
"We would rather it would rain ... but we should be able to mitigate a good proportion of the potential problems," he said.

Southcorp Wines' Kemp was cautious, saying 15-20 percent of Southcorp's vineyards relied on run-off water but stressing it was too early for predictions for a vintage which will be not be properly underway until March 1998.
